analysis.one_liner: Removes new monopoly protections for old biologic drugs like insulin, speeding cheaper copies to market.
analysis.headline: With one Democrat and two Republicans attached, the bill died in the Senate Health Committee without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Insulin and a few other drugs were historically approved as ordinary drugs, but on March 23, 2020 the law switched them to the stricter "biologic" pathway. Without this bill, those products could count as brand-new biologics and claim the 12-year monopoly period that blocks approval of cheaper biosimilar copies. This bill says products that were first approved under the old drug pathway — insulin is the example the official summary gives — get no such fresh monopoly, so cheaper follow-on versions could be approved sooner.
analysis.who_benefits: People who rely on insulin and similar long-marketed drugs, plus anyone who would benefit from more biosimilar competition, since it would deny brand-name makers a new 12-year monopoly window on products that had already been on the market for years, clearing the way for cheaper copies to be licensed under the biosimilar pathway sooner [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Blocks products that were first approved under the old drug pathway — insulin is the example the official summary gives — from being treated as newly licensed biologics for purposes of the exclusivity periods that delay approval of biosimilar copies under the biosimilar pathway.

Applies the existing limit on exclusivity to any reference product, whether it was originally licensed as a biologic or merely deemed one during the 2020 transition, so no old product gets a fresh monopoly clock.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name makers of insulin and the other affected products, who lose the chance to count a new licensing date toward years of market exclusivity and would face biosimilar competition sooner [S2] [S3]. The public pays nothing directly under the bill; the cost falls on the brand manufacturers' future monopoly revenue.

drawbacks.text: Biologic exclusivity exists to reward companies for the large cost of developing and testing these drugs; narrowing it, even for transition-period products, reduces that incentive at the margin — the trade-off an honest supporter would acknowledge.

The bill is narrow: it touches only products deemed licensed during the 2020 transition and does nothing about the 12-year exclusivity that brand biologics licensed under the normal pathway keep, so it would not by itself change prices for most biologic drugs.
Even without exclusivity, follow-on insulin developers would still face costly FDA testing and approval requirements, so cheaper versions would not appear overnight.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the potential gain is real but modest in scope: it removes one legal barrier to cheaper insulin-style competition for a specific set of transitioned products. The cost falls almost entirely on a handful of brand manufacturers' future monopoly revenue, with a marginal trade-off in development incentives. The bill was not flawed so much as unfinished business — it sat untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Tina Smith introduced the bill on April 11, 2019, joined by two Republican cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The committee took no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the 116th Congress, which ended January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name makers of insulin and similar long-marketed biologics are better off: by dying in committee, the bill left their exclusivity protections untouched, and patients kept paying the same high prices.

for.name: Tina Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate HELP Committee.

for.name: Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, one of two Republican cosponsors.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; the record shows no action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat sponsored it with two Republican cosponsors, but no hearing or vote was ever held, so no partisan split on the bill was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have denied products like insulin a fresh 12-year exclusivity clock when they were deemed licensed as biologics, exposing them to biosimilar competition sooner and costing them monopoly revenue. Their interest in blocking the bill ran directly against patients' interest in cheaper versions.

The bill would have opened a faster path to FDA approval of biosimilar copies of transitioned products, expanding the market for follow-on manufacturers. Their gain would come through lower prices for patients.
